 Daylight Saving Time has become somewhat of a hot topic, with efforts to stop the clock (well, at least from changing) and make Daylight Saving Time the new permanent standard time in the U.S. The Sunshine Protection Act of 2025 is waiting for Senate approval. 
 In a poll of nearly 50,000 people, 69% of respondents said they support permanent Daylight Saving Time. 
 Other than the shift in your daily routine, many people are not a fan of the dark mornings, missing the early morning sunlight. 
 But with the recent "Fall Back" bringing earlier sunrises, those living inside the polar circles are currently seeing no sunrise! 
 The Arctic Circle and the Antarctic Circle experience what's called "polar night."
 Polar night is when the sun does not rise above the horizon for more than 24 hours. 
 Due to Earth's tilted axis, one hemisphere will be tilted away from the sun for part of the year, meaning no sunlight during the whole day. 
 During the December solstice, the Arctic Circle (Norway, Alaska, Canada, Greenland, Finland, etc.) experiences this, between September and March. The closer you are to the poles, the longer the polar night lasts. 
 Svalbard, Norway is one of the longest populated polar nights, lasting about four months. 
 This doesn't mean it's pitch black the whole time. 
 The lack of sunshine makes for ideal conditions to see the Northern Lights, or aurora borealis. 
 Then around the Spring Equinox, it's the polar opposite - 24-hour sunshine in the Northern Hemisphere (polar night in the Southern Hemisphere).
